title: Planning for Emergence
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: Nickhart argues that the standard school improvement planning model—define goals, specify actions, set success criteria, monitor progress—rests on a faulty premise: that complex systems like schools respond to inputs predictably enough for linear cause-and-effect planning to work. As an alternative, he introduces 'planning for emergence'—holding desired outcomes in mind while accepting that improvement will unfold through interpretation and interaction rather than predictable sequencing, because outcomes in complex systems are genuinely difficult to predict even when patterns of behavior are not. The key strategic shift is upstream: away from refining action lists and tightening monitoring, and toward the conditions that shape behavior—trusting relationships, individual intellectual capacity, and organizational capacity to learn. Common SIP actions (deliver CPD, implement consistent strategy, monitor through learning walks) are not wrong in themselves, but they reveal a 'technical problem' mindset that misses the deeper cultural conditions that will determine their success. The leader's role in a complex system is to sustain attention on what is emerging, adapt when the system pushes back, and notice leverage opportunities—spending less time perfecting documents and more time strengthening shared understanding and building the quality of thinking across the organization.
points: School improvement plans implicitly assume linear cause-and-effect in a system that doesn't offer it; planning for emergence accepts that improvements arise through the interaction of people, ideas, and context—not faithful execution of a predetermined sequence.

The most important improvement drivers (trusting relationships, individual knowledge, organizational learning capacity) are typically the least visible items in a school improvement plan, which focuses on deliverables and monitoring instead.

The harder the improvement plan is pushed, the more the system adapts to resist: cause-and-effect becomes difficult to trace, compliance-monitoring substitutes for iterative learning, and the plan's structure prevents it from detecting its own failures.

The leader's role in complexity is fundamentally different: sustain attention on what is emerging, adapt when the system pushes back, notice leverage opportunities—less time perfecting documents, more time strengthening shared understanding and improving thinking quality.

Plans still matter for coordination, communication, and accountability—but the real improvement work happens in how people interpret the plan, interact with each other in response to it, and what those interactions actually change.
quotes: Much of what sits inside a typical school improvement plan assumes a level of predictability that the system simply doesn't offer. Goals are defined. Actions are specified. Success criteria are set. Progress is monitored. It is a necessary structure, but it is built on an assumption that if we do the right things, in the right order, we will produce the intended outcomes. And we know, from experience, that it doesn't quite work like that.

Planning for emergence might hold those same desired outcomes in mind but accepts that they will not unfold in a predictable sequence. It recognises that actions are interpreted and adapted as the team goes about its work, with improvements emerging from the interaction between people, ideas and context.

If improvement emerges through patterns of interaction and interpretation, then planning needs to create the conditions in which better patterns are more likely. And what are these conditions? Trusting relationships, intellectual capacity of individuals, organisational capacity to learn.

The role of the leader is fundamentally different if the system is complex, not complicated. If cause and effect are distant, the task is to sustain attention on what is emerging. If systems push back, the task is to adapt in response to how the system is behaving. If small changes can produce large effects, the task is to notice leverage opportunities.

Spend less time perfecting documents (though they still matter for governance and accountability) and spend more time strengthening shared understanding. Spend less time on tracking whether actions are completed (but this is still important) and spend more time on whether thinking is improving.
The real work happens in how people interpret that plan, how they interact with each other in response to it, and how those interactions shape what actually changes.
